q1_feeder_simulation_methods.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. Which physics-based simulation methods have been used to model screw or auger feeders and the micro-dosing of powders: DEM with any contact model, coupled CFD-DEM, continuum approaches (material point method, SPH, FEM with Drucker-Prager or mu(I) rheology), cellular automata, and analytical or reduced-order feed-factor models? For each method give the codes used (open-source such as LIGGGHTS, LAMMPS granular, MercuryDPM, Yade, Project Chrono, MFiX, Blaze-DEM, or commercial such as EDEM, Rocky, PFC), the contact and cohesion models, speed-ups (coarse-graining, reduced Young's modulus, GPU), typical computational cost, what was validated against experiments (mass flow rate, feed factor, fluctuations, refill), and which studies used the simulation to infer powder properties from feeder data. Rank the methods by suitability for a millimetre-scale auger dosing cohesive fine powders (10-100 micrometres) and salts, and list concrete published input parameters we could reuse.

Project scope: the work is one manuscript for the journal Additive Manufacturing with a conference talk in mid-March 2027, one graduate student plus AI agents, one doser, and simulation compute of a 4-core cloud runner (a 48-run DEM design costs about 96 CPU-hours). Calibration today is multi-objective Bayesian optimization (Ax; Sobol screening, then SAASBO with qNEHVI) of eight controller settings (bulk and trickle tilt, tap tilt, bulk speed, two tap on/off choices, the switch point to trickle feeding and the stopping band) to minimize dose time and error; salt took 42 doses (20 screening, 14 chosen by the optimizer, 8 validation) and gave 0.5 g in a median 78 s with 1.8 mg error, against 245 s hand-tuned. A multi-task Gaussian process across powders (a task-index kernel plus a descriptor kernel built from the dosing fingerprint) is planned for metal powders (AlSi10Mg, Al 4047, 316L, 630 bronze, Al 6063 and lab-atomized custom alloys). In-house tests are angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, Hall and Carney funnels, moisture sensitivity by dosing before and after exposure to humid air, and PSD from SEM or laser diffraction; shear-cell ffc has to be outsourced. Our team needs a clear, step-by-step picture of how a physics-based simulator would help us (a) infer the properties of a new powder from its dosing data and (b) calibrate the doser's settings for a new powder with fewer doses. Lay out such a workflow end to end and, for each step, cite published examples and give typical numbers of simulations and experiments: (1) which simulator parameters stand for which powder properties (sliding and rolling friction, surface energy or granular Bond number, capillary or moisture terms) and how each maps to measurable quantities (angle of repose, Hausner ratio, shear-cell ffc, Hall flow, moisture content); (2) designing the simulation runs and building an emulator of the dosing fingerprint (Gaussian process, polynomial chaos, neural network); (3) Bayesian calibration of a new powder's parameters from its measured fingerprint, with a model-discrepancy term (Kennedy-O'Hagan) and identifiability checks, including synthetic recovery of known parameters; (4) using the calibrated parameters to predict the powder's behaviour in standard tests and in blade spreading, and how that has been validated; (5) using the simulator to speed up Bayesian optimization of feeder or dosing settings for a new material, for example as a prior mean function, as a low-fidelity source in multi-fidelity BO, as physics-based task descriptors in multi-task or transfer-learning BO, or to narrow the search space, with any published evidence of how many experiments this saves compared with single-task BO or with carrying over the settings of the most similar material. Then propose a feasibility test that fits our scope: the smallest set of simulations, powders and measurements that would show whether the simulator adds value, explicit go/no-go criteria, the simplest baselines it must beat (for example a direct statistical mapping from the dosing fingerprint to measured properties with no simulator, a closed-form Beverloo outlet model, and single-task BO), and which results would tell us to drop the simulator from the paper.

Our data so far: 13 powders (NaCl, Si 75-150 um and Si <44 um, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg, Na2SO4, BaCl2 dihydrate, calcium lactate, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, sodium alginate, white and brown rice flour, fumed silica), each run once through a fixed protocol on a cone-exit auger: mass per revolution at 0, 22.5 and 45 degree tube tilt (30 rpm, six single revolutions each), a speed exponent from 15 to 90 rpm, mass released per solenoid tap, mass that flows during a 15 s static hold, and closed-loop doses of 50, 200 and 1000 mg (error, time, pass rate). Mass per revolution spans more than three decades and five powders barely convey. The property values we have are handbook or supplier values for each material class (angle of repose, bulk and tapped density, Hausner ratio, d50, true density, equilibrium moisture), not measurements on our lots, and their published ranges are wide (angle of repose ranges 6-16 degrees). Literature angle of repose correlates with log mass per revolution at 45 degrees (Spearman -0.84); d50 and Hausner ratio do not. We plan to measure angle of repose, PSD, bulk and tapped density and moisture on the same jars, to add powders (metal AM powders, sieved size fractions, humidity-conditioned salt), and we have the DEM twin described above. Questions: (1) Which published studies built statistical or machine-learning models that predict feeder or doser performance (feed factor, mass flow rate, flow variability, feeding capacity, refill behaviour, dosing accuracy) from raw-material properties, for example material property libraries with PCA or PLS for loss-in-weight, screw and micro-feeders, and which studies predicted powder properties (flowability class, ffc, Hausner ratio, cohesion, particle size, moisture) from process or flow signals (feeder, rotating drum or avalanche tester, vibrating capillary, hopper or funnel discharge)? For each, give the number of materials, the descriptors and responses, the model, the validation scheme and the accuracy reached. (2) For datasets of 10-40 materials, which model classes and practices work best (PLS, ridge or lasso, Gaussian processes, random forests, gradient boosting, neural networks, Bayesian latent-variable or multi-output models, monotone or physics-constrained models)? How should repeated measurements per material, censored responses (no flow), and noisy or literature-derived property labels be handled, and how should models be validated (leave-one-material-out, nested cross-validation, prospective tests on new materials)? (3) How have physics-based models (DEM, Beverloo, Jenike or screw-conveyor models) been combined with data-driven models in this setting: simulation-generated training data, physics-informed features such as granular Bond number or orifice-to-particle size ratio, residual or discrepancy learning, multi-fidelity or transfer learning, and with what measured gains? (4) How many materials and which measurements are typically needed to reach useful accuracy, and which descriptors have proven most predictive of flow in small feeders (cohesion or ffc, wall friction, bulk density, PSD width, particle shape, moisture, electrostatics)? (5) How can a model that predicts properties from dosing data and a model that predicts dosing from properties be kept consistent (one joint latent-variable model, Bayesian inversion of a forward model, or two separate regressions), and have such models been used to choose initial settings, priors or task descriptors for Bayesian optimization of feeding or dosing for a new material?
